title: CEPI Gives Pune's Immunoscript $8.9M for Freezer-Free RNA Vaccines
excerpt: The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations will fund Pune-based Immunoscript Life Science with up to $8.9 million to advance clinical testing of its thermostable self-amplifying RNA vaccine platform — a key piece of the global '100 Days Mission' to prepare for Disease X.
body:
• The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) will provide up to $8.9 million (almost ₹85 crore) to Pune-based Immunoscript Life Science to advance clinical testing of its thermostable, "freezer-free" self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine platform.
  • The nanoemulsion-based platform — developed and authorized in India during the COVID-19 pandemic — could remain stable without deep freezing, removing the cold-chain barrier that strands vaccines before they reach remote communities.
  • The project feeds CEPI's "100 Days Mission," backed by India and other G20 and G7 nations, to develop vaccines against emerging threats — including a future "Disease X" — within 100 days of identification.
  • Immunoscript will first test the platform as a prototype next-generation rabies vaccine, with early Phase I human trials expected within about six months of regulatory approval in India.

A 69-day-old company wins a global vote of confidence

Immunoscript Life Science is barely months into operation — yet it has just landed one of the most significant vaccine R&D grants an Indian biotech has received this year. The Oslo-based Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations announced funding of up to $8.9 million for the Pune company to advance clinical testing of its thermostable self-amplifying RNA vaccine platform, which could be deployed in communities where cold-chain infrastructure is limited.

"It is day 69 since the start of the company, and the company received its first funding," Dr Sanjay Singh, Immunoscript's founder and chief executive, told The Hindu BusinessLine. Singh is the former chief executive of Gennova Biopharmaceuticals, the company behind India's only mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. Gennova is a subsidiary of Emcure Pharma, and less than two months ago it transferred its mRNA business to the fledgling Immunoscript.

Why freezer-free matters

Messenger RNA vaccines were the defining technology of the COVID-19 response — fast and flexible in design compared with traditional approaches. But they carry a stubborn weakness: conventional mRNA formulations must be stored and transported at ultra-low temperatures to stay stable and effective. During an outbreak, that requirement can block doses from reaching low-resource or remote settings that lack the equipment to keep them from spoiling.

According to estimates from the World Health Organization cited by the UK Health Security Agency, roughly half of all vaccines globally fail to reach their intended populations because of these logistical breakdowns. A formulation that holds up without deep freezing would cut the cost and complexity of distribution — and could be the difference between containment and catastrophe when a new pathogen emerges.

Immunoscript's platform, called CLNE, uses a nanoemulsion design that CEPI describes as a world-first technology capable of delivering freezer-free RNA vaccines. The investment will let the company further develop the platform through early human testing, with Phase I safety trials slated to begin once Indian regulators grant approval — tentatively within six months, Singh said.

Rabies first, Disease X next

The company has been tasked with proving the platform against a possible unknown disease, and it is starting with a concrete target: a next-generation rabies vaccine. Since a new-generation rabies vaccine is needed, Singh said, the team is testing the platform against rabies — the pathogen will serve as a prototype to demonstrate that the technology works against diseases beyond COVID-19.

The work is considered pivotal to the 100 Days Mission, the campaign spearheaded by CEPI and backed by India and other G20 and G7 nations to develop vaccines against emerging diseases in as little as 100 days. "This could better prepare both India and the world against deadly emerging threats including a future 'Disease X'," CEPI chief executive Richard Hatchett said in announcing the funding.

"Advances in RNA-vaccine technology were critical to the global response to COVID-19 and will be crucial for future epidemic and pandemic responses."

— Dr Melanie Saville, Executive Director of Vaccine R&D, CEPI

India's growing RNA medicine sector

The funding marks an important boost to India's RNA medicine sector, which has been building on its pandemic-era foundations. Gennova's earlier mRNA work — including two COVID-19 vaccines that received emergency authorization in India — was supported by the Department of Biotechnology through the Ind-CEPI Mission under the COVID-19 Consortium, establishing a manufacturing and R&D base that Immunoscript now inherits.

Singh pointed to Gennova's decade of collaborations with institutions including the US FDA, NIH, Johns Hopkins and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine as the groundwork that let the company build a pandemic-ready mRNA manufacturing platform. The CEPI deal commits Immunoscript to technology transfer as well, aligning with the coalition's push for equitable access.

Diaspora angle

The Indian diaspora felt the cold-chain problem personally during COVID-19: families arranging vaccinations for elderly parents in hometowns, and diaspora-funded relief efforts that ran into the same logistics wall. A thermostable RNA platform developed in India — transferable to other countries — directly addresses that inequity. And for the thousands of Indian-origin scientists and biotech professionals working in Boston, the Bay Area and London, the grant signals that India's vaccine R&D ecosystem is moving from contract manufacturing toward platform innovation.

What's next

The immediate milestone is regulatory: Immunoscript needs Indian approvals to start its early Phase I safety trials, which Singh tentatively places about six months out. If the rabies prototype validates the platform, the technology would enter CEPI's broader Disease X preparedness toolkit — a thermostable, rapidly adaptable vaccine engine that could be reprogrammed against whatever pathogen comes next.

nri_angle: For the Indian diaspora — many of whom flew relatives home for COVID shots or funded vaccine drives — a thermostable RNA platform built in India could one day mean outbreak response that reaches grandparents in villages as fast as it reaches cities.
